job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Bilal Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live at home in Leicester, above my parents' corner shop, which makes mornings loud. I'm up at six to help with deliveries, then I drive to Loughborough for my master's in robotics and AI. After lectures I work on a stock-ordering app I built for the shop, and I'm now trying it with two other shops on our street. Last summer I did ten weeks at a warehouse automation company, tuning picking software. I use AI tools all day, for code, for planning, even for drafting emails to suppliers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a letdown for the hype crowd, but fine for me. I'd tell friends the tools are great helpers, so use them, but nobody's job vanishes. Online I'd probably share a few tips, because people ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm already ahead of most people because I use the tools daily. A plateau means that edge lasts. The only worry is the usual one: loans, about eighteen thousand, and a job market where I haven't landed yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the master's, keep building the app and sign up three more shops. I'd apply to about twenty jobs in warehouse automation and robotics, and see which gives a better offer. I'd keep helping in the shop on weekends, because my parents need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. I've got a skill, a side project and a family that backs me. Nothing in that world scares me, apart from my own impatience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the other two shops that use your app.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two other shops on our street pay thirty a month each now, which shows my stock-ordering app works for people who aren't my parents. It's not much. My dad thinks it's a hobby, but he's started asking me to add a feature for sell-by dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the app grows?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd treat it as a business, not a hobby. If I get to five shops, I'll talk to a small business adviser. Dad's friend Mr Rahman did that and it helped him a lot.

I'd share a few **tips** online, because people ask.
think: I'm already **ahead** of most people because I use the tools daily.
The only worry is the usual one: about **eighteen thousand** in loans.
do: Finish the master's and sign up **three more shops**.
Apply to about **twenty** automation and robotics jobs.
Help in my parents' **shop** at weekends.
feel: I feel **calm**; I've got a skill, a side project and a family behind me.

steps.text: Sign up three more local shops for the stock-ordering app
Apply to about twenty warehouse automation and robotics employers
Help in the family shop at weekends and finish the master's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's good news and bad news. The tools will do more, and the people who learn to direct them will do well. I'd say learn now and don't wait for the company to teach you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it favours people like me, who already work with them. But I'd be foolish to think I'm safe, because coding is on the card's list. Junior coders will be fewer, and I'm one. The advantage is that I'm also hands-on with robots and shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the app harder, adding ordering for suppliers and a simple AI forecast of what sells. I'd also apply for jobs in warehouse automation, where software meets machines. And I'd try to turn a couple of the shops into proper customers, with a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit uneasy. There's a thrill to it, but I can see my friends from the course, who aren't using the tools, are going to struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell friends who aren't using the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say start with one tool for one task, like having it explain your code. Then do another one the next week. It sounds trivial, but I watched my cousin do it and he went from sceptic to user in a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you worry about for the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' shop. If a chain opens near my parents' shop and has an AI that handles stock perfectly, it's hard to compete. That's why I'm pushing the app, because small shops need tools too.

I'm also **hands-on** with robots and shops.

Turn two shops into **proper customers** with a contract.

fieldNote: Bilal reads the card as **opportunity** with a real risk for junior coders.

steps.text: Add supplier ordering and a simple sales forecast to the app

Apply for warehouse automation jobs where software meets machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hold on, because two years is very fast. I'd want shops, schools and councils to get help to adopt it. I'd be saying to people, use the tools to protect yourself, because the others will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be worried. A lot of what I do on screen, a system could do quicker. My advantage is physical: warehouses and robots, which come a few years later. I'd lean hard on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the robotics side and on the app, selling it to as many shops as I can. I'd take the first job that puts me near real machines, even if the pay is low. I'd stay at home, save and tell my parents to cut the shop's risks by watching stock more carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I won't pretend otherwise. Part of me thinks this is when people like me matter, and another part thinks the thing I'm good at gets cheaper by the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about the family side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the family. My parents rely on the shop and I've got a younger sister, Amna, in sixth form. I'd say that if the worst happened, the shop is the safety net, but a shop depends on customers who have jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything outside your usual habits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I think we'd need some kind of income support or council help for small shops. I'd write to my MP and join a shopkeepers' group. I don't normally do that, but this isn't a normal situation.

I'd tell people to use the tools to **protect themselves**.

My advantage is **physical**: warehouses and robots come a few years later.

S2.quote: Part of me thinks this is when people like me matter, and another part thinks the thing I'm good at gets cheaper by the week.
fieldNote: Bilal's **adaptive** side turns fear into action, with warehouses as his bet.
His **family shop** is a safety net with its own risk.
He would break habit and **join a shopkeepers' group**.

steps.text: Sell the stock-ordering app to as many local shops as possible
Take the first job working near real warehouse robots
Stay at home and save most of my pay
Join a local shopkeepers' association and write to my MP

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good window to learn and build. I'd tell my class to start building things, not just studying. At the shop I'd say let's try new tools one at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have about four good years in the field by 2031, with the app maybe a real business. If the app is earning, I'd have something that isn't a job. That's the plan, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the master's, take a job in warehouse automation and keep the app going on evenings. I'd save about a third of my pay and invest a bit in an index fund. I'd also try to hire a part-time helper for the app by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but positive. Five years feels like a fair fight. I think I'd be energised, because it gives me time to be ahead of the curve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check to know the app is working as a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one risk is that all this effort leaves me with a lot of software and no real business. I'd test it by asking the shops each quarter if they'd pay more, and if they won't, I'd stop and take the job full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would say take the job and forget the app. Mum would say follow your gut. I'd probably do both, which is my usual way.

Save a third of my pay for the first four years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so no one should panic. I'd tell friends to learn the tools now, then use the time to find the thing they're good at. At the shop I'd say we'd have enough time to rebuild the business around the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. I'd be thirty-four with a decade of practice with the tools, maybe running a small company. I'd be hiring people who haven't used them yet, rather than competing with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the master's, take a good job, and build the app into a business over the first three years. I'd buy a flat when I'm about thirty, and I'd invest steadily. I'd also help my sister Amna choose a degree that's about people as well as screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited. Ten years is plenty. I'd be spending my energy on the thing I like, which is building, and not on worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister Amna about her degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister Amna to do a mix: something technical, like engineering, and something human, like design or care. And to learn the tools in her first year, before she needs them. She's sharper than me, so she'll probably do better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the shop over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop. Ten years from now there might be a chain, or a robot shelf stacker. My parents will be near retirement, so I'd want to plan to sell or hand over the shop in good shape, not in a rush.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because even I couldn't be sure my skills stay valuable in two years. What would help is shops getting some help to adopt the tools, flexible loan repayments and early honest warnings. I'd also want my parents' shop to stay in good shape.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think using AI all day makes me a fan. I'm not a fan, I'm a user. I'd just rather be the one holding the tool than the one it replaces.

headlineQuote: I'm not a fan, I'm a user. I'd just rather be the one holding the tool than the one it replaces.
portrait: Bilal is a **24-year-old** robotics and AI master's student who lives above his parents' corner shop in Leicester.
He uses AI tools **every day** and has built a stock-ordering app that three shops now use.
He owes about **eighteen thousand**, and his parents back him but rely on the shop.
As a pragmatic centrist, he judges each scenario by what's **practical** and spreads risk across a job, the app and savings.
He stays **calm** in most worlds and turns anxious only when AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because even his skills could lose value fast and his family's shop would be exposed.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **small shops** to adopt tools, flexible loan repayments and early, honest warnings.
